content: Granulin is a protein encoded by the GRN gene in humans. It is a 5 kDa protein. Although the precise functions of progranulin and granulin remain unclear, both forms of the protein have been implicated in critical biological processes such as development, inflammation, cell proliferation, and protein homeostasis. The discovery in 2006 of GRN mutations in patients with frontotemporal dementia has driven extensive research into the role of progranulin in disease and its broader physiological functions. While research on progranulin's role in the body is expanding, studies focusing on specific granulin residues remain limited. Progranulin serves as the precursor protein for granulin. Proteolytic cleavage of progranulin generates various active 6 kDa granulin peptides, which are designated as granulin A, granulin B, granulin C, and so on. Epithelins 1 and 2 are synonymous with granulins A and B, respectively. This cleavage occurs either in the extracellular matrix or within lysosomes. Proteases such as elastase, proteinase 3, and matrix metalloproteinases are capable of cleaving progranulin into individual granulin peptides. Progranulin and granulin exhibit opposing roles in cellular processes: progranulin is associated with anti-inflammatory effects, whereas cleaved granulin peptides are linked to pro-inflammatory activity. Studies in C. elegans suggest that granulin peptides may also exhibit toxic properties. Progranulin is expressed in a wide range of cell types, both in peripheral tissues and the central nervous system. Its expression is low during early development but increases as cells mature. Cell types expressing progranulin include neurons, microglia, astrocytes, and endothelial cells. Progranulin is particularly highly expressed in microglia and is upregulated during injury. Within the brain, progranulin mRNA is abundantly expressed in pyramidal cells, hippocampal cells, and Purkinje cells. Each individual granulin domain peptide consists of 60 amino acids and is rich in cysteine residues, allowing the formation of six disulfide bonds per residue. These disulfide bonds create a central rod-like core that organizes each granulin peptide into a stacked β-sheet configuration. The structure of granulin proteins resembles that of proteins from families involved in hormones, growth factors, ion channel modulators, and enzyme inhibitors. Due to these structural similarities, significant research has been conducted to explore progranulin's potential role as a growth factor. When secreted into the extracellular matrix, progranulin is often glycosylated at four confirmed and one tentative N-linked glycosylation sites. The N-terminus of progranulin is hypothesized to play a role in its secretion via secretory vesicles, potentially regulating exosome excretion. The C-terminus is thought to be the primary binding partner of SORT1, a receptor for extracellular progranulin. However, the structural differences between individual granulin peptides remain to be fully characterized. In the extracellular matrix, progranulin binds to receptors on various cell types, leading to either activation of signal transduction pathways or cellular engulfment. Progranulin has been shown to interact with SORT1, mediating the trafficking of bound progranulin to lysosomes. Recent studies suggest that progranulin may also facilitate prosaposin trafficking to lysosomes via SORT1. However, the absence of SORT1 does not prevent exogenous progranulin from promoting neurite outgrowth or enhancing cell survival in GRN knockout cells, indicating the involvement of other receptors in mediating extracellular progranulin functions. For instance, SORT1-deficient neuronal cells can still bind progranulin. Other studies have proposed tumor necrosis factor and EPH receptor A2 as potential facilitators of progranulin activity. After receptor binding, progranulin may induce and modulate signaling pathways such as MAPK/ERK, PI3K/Akt, and FAK. Gene ontology enrichment analysis has also linked progranulin to Notch receptor signaling. Granulin has been shown to interact with Cyclin T1 and TRIB3. Progranulin plays a role in development, as its expression increases with cell maturation. It is hypothesized to act as a neurotrophic factor involved in corticogenesis. Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines harboring GRN mutations exhibit reduced cortical neuronal differentiation capacity. In mice, progranulin has been implicated in regulating early cerebellar development by selecting individual climbing fibers as they intersect and form synapses with Purkinje cells. Additionally, progranulin is involved in synaptic pruning, a microglial process essential for neural network development. Cytokines, markers of synapse elimination, are upregulated in neurons with GRN mutations, leading to increased microglial density and activity around synapses. Progranulin may also play a role in sexual determination during embryonic development. Progranulin levels are elevated during tissue inflammation. Following wounding, keratinocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils increase progranulin production. Neutrophils secrete elastase into the extracellular matrix, which cleaves progranulin into granulin peptides that further promote inflammation. Neutrophils and macrophages also release SLPI, an elastase inhibitor, to modulate progranulin cleavage. The addition of granulin B to cultured epithelial cells induces the secretion of IL-8, a chemokine that attracts monocytes and neutrophils, further supporting the pro-inflammatory role of granulin peptides. Exogenous SLPI and progranulin can mitigate the heightened inflammatory response in mice unable to inhibit progranulin cleavage. Progranulin is highly expressed in cells with high proliferative activity. It has been implicated in tumorigenesis and neuronal outgrowth. Progranulin promotes mitogenesis in epithelial cultures, and its addition to epithelial cell lines stimulates proliferation. In zebrafish models, knocking out progranulin homologs reduces axonal outgrowth. In primary cortical and motor neurons, progranulin regulates neuronal outgrowth and survival. Specifically, in motor neurons, progranulin enhances neurite outgrowth by modulating glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta. Progranulin may function as an autocrine growth factor in tumorigenesis. The discovery of GRN mutations associated with lysosomal storage disorders has spurred research into progranulin's role in protein homeostasis via the lysosomal pathway. Transcriptomic studies suggest that progranulin is heavily involved in lysosomal function and organization. Imaging studies have shown co-localization of progranulin with the lysosomal marker LAMP-1. Progranulin expression is regulated by TFEB, a transcription factor mediating lysosomal biosynthesis. Progranulin may also regulate protease activity, including prosaposin cleavage into saposin peptides and cathepsin D, a key protease in protein aggregate breakdown. GRN mutations share neuropathological and clinical features with CHMP2B and VCP mutations, genes involved in lysosomal trafficking and protein degradation. Heterozygous mutations in the GRN gene, leading to progranulin haploinsufficiency, cause frontotemporal dementia (FTD). These mutations include frameshift, splice site, nonsense, signal peptide, Kozak sequence disruptions, and missense mutations, resulting in either nonsense-mediated decay or non-functional protein production. GRN-FTD patients exhibit asymmetric brain atrophy, with variability in age of onset, disease progression, and clinical symptoms, suggesting additional genetic or environmental factors influence disease expression. Pathological indicators include cytosolic ubiquitin deposits enriched in hyperphosphorylated TDP-43, autophagy-related protein aggregates, ubiquitin-binding protein p62, lentiform intranuclear inclusions, dystrophic neurites, and inflammation. GRN mutation carriers show a 70-80% reduction in serum progranulin levels compared to controls. Reprogrammed stem cells restore GRN mRNA levels to 50%, further implicating other factors in FTD regulation. Mice with GRN mutations exhibit reduced autophagic flux and clearance, while human FTD-GRN fibroblasts show decreased lysosomal protease activity and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis-like storage material. FTD-GRN iPSC-derived cortical neurons display enlarged vesicles, lipofuscin accumulation, and cathepsin D deficiency. Homozygous GRN mutations cause neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL), characterized by autofluorescent lipofuscin accumulation, enlarged vacuoles, impaired lysosomal activity, retinal and brain degeneration, exaggerated inflammatory responses, microgliosis, astrogliosis, and behavioral dysfunctions such as OCD-like and disinhibition-like behaviors. Aged GRN double mutant mice exhibit lipofuscin deposits, enlarged lysosomes, and phosphorylated TDP-43 in some cases. Progranulin may also contribute to cancer development, atherosclerosis, and metabolic diseases. It promotes Cyclin D1 expression in breast cancer lines and protein phosphorylation via extracellular-regulated kinase signaling pathways. Progranulin is highly expressed in ovarian and adrenal carcinomas and immortalized epithelial cells. There is a correlation between progranulin concentration and cancer severity. Granulin release by macrophages has been associated with fibrotic hepatic metastasis in pancreatic cancer. The human liver fluke (Opisthorchis viverrini) contributes to bile duct cancer by secreting a granulin-like growth hormone. Progranulin may also promote atherosclerosis progression, with progranulin being anti-atherogenic and granulins being pro-atherogenic. Increased serum and plasma progranulin levels in patients with type 2 diabetes and visceral obesity implicate progranulin in metabolic diseases.
